1 · Peng–Robinson flash vs an independent implementation

Engine: the flash drum with the flowsheet's default property method, Peng–Robinson (the rigorous unit a new flowsheet uses). Reference: the open-source thermo 0.6.1 library (Gibbs-stability flash with PR gas and liquid phases), given the same ChemSep critical constants (true H₂ constants), acentric factors and binary interaction parameters. This verifies the φ–φ flash itself; how well Peng–Robinson matches experiment depends on the kij values, which can be tuned.

2 · Peng–Robinson flash vs DWSIM

Reference: DWSIM 9.0.5, the open-source process simulator (Peng–Robinson property package, default flash), run through its automation interface on the same six feeds.

Classic flash drum on the same equation of state

The classic flash drum (property method Classic, flash model Peng–Robinson) used to carry its own copy of the equation of state, with effective H₂ constants (43.6 K / 20.5 bar / 0) and a short kij table. It now calls the same Peng–Robinson package as the rigorous units — ChemSep constants, the kij databank, free water, stability test and Newton fallback — so the two agree; the small remaining differences come only from the molar masses each path uses to turn the mass-based feed into mole fractions:

The engine's default method and DWSIM now start from the same ChemSep constants; the inputs still differ in kij CH4–H2. The separator vapour carries 2.842 mol % NH₃ in the engine and 2.842 mol % in DWSIM; dissolved H₂ is 0.602 against 0.602 mol %. Neither program has data for H₂–NH₃ or CH₄–NH₃ (kij = 0 in both; the engine says so in its run warnings), and the NH₃ left in loop gas is sensitive to them. This comparison does not show which set is closer to a real loop; for loop work, calibrate those kij against plant separator analyses (Methods → binary data).

3 · NRTL activity coefficients

The engine's NRTL flash against an independent calculation: thermo's NRTL model for γ (Aspen form τij = aij + bij/T, α = 0.3; parameters are test inputs, not a recommended data set). In the two-phase case the liquid composition is solved independently as well, from the bubble condition Σ xiγiPsat,i = P with the IAPWS-IF97 water vapour pressure (iapws library) and the ethanol Antoine constants the engine lists.

4 · Energy balance with condensation

20 mol % steam in N2/CO2 at 150 °C / 5 bar + N2 at 25 °C → cooler 40 °C → knock-out 4.8 bar. Engine: rigorous mixer, heater and flash drum with the default property method (Peng–Robinson, free water on). Reference: CoolProp 8.0 (IAPWS-95 water, reference equations of state for N₂ and CO₂) evaluated at the component partial pressures with a Raoult split at the drum.

QuantityEngineReferenceDifference
Total heat removed, kW-312.0-313.20.37 %
Condensate, kg/h331.2332.20.29 %

The reference splits the drum by Raoult's law (no gas-phase non-ideality). Peng–Robinson leaves slightly more water in the gas at 4.8 bar — an enhancement factor of a few per cent, which the plain cubic's water–N₂ attraction (kij = 0) somewhat overstates — hence the small condensate difference. Without free water the duty is 3.2 % off.

7 · Three-phase (VLLE) and liquid–liquid flash

The three-phase separator, and every flash when the method's valid phases include a second liquid, tests the two-phase answer for another liquid (Michelsen tangent-plane distance), converges vapour, light liquid and heavy liquid with a three-phase Rachford–Rice, and keeps the state with the lowest Gibbs energy. References: thermo's FlashVLN (one Peng–Robinson gas and two Peng–Robinson liquids, same constants and kij) for water–hydrocarbon systems, and isoactivity equations solved separately with thermo's activity models for partially miscible liquids.

10 · Phase envelopes vs DWSIM

Bubble and dew curves traced by Michelsen's continuation method (Newton on ln K, ln T and ln P with the most sensitive variable specified, stepping through the critical point), with the critical point located on the curve and the cricondenbar / cricondentherm refined. Reference: DWSIM 9.0.5 with the same critical constants and kij — its critical point from the Heidemann–Khalil method, its cricondentherm as the hottest point of its own dew curve (sampled every 0.5 bar). Points along the traced curves were also confirmed with independent bubble / dew calculations in thermo to within 2·10⁻⁴ K.

12 · Kinetic plug-flow and CSTR reactors vs exact solutions

Power-law kinetics in the chosen phase of the property method. The plug-flow reactor integrates molar flows and enthalpy flow (Dormand–Prince RK5(4), switching to the L-stable Rosenbrock method RODAS3 when the kinetics are stiff); the CSTR solves the extents and temperature by Newton from several starts, reports every steady state it finds, and takes very fast kinetics to the steady state by pseudo-transient continuation. References: Levenspiel's closed forms for first-order reactions with volume change, scipy LSODA and root-bracketing on the same ideal-gas balances (adiabatic, cooled and fixed-duty reactors, including all three steady states of an exothermic CSTR), the closed-form solution of a linear system with a stiffness ratio of 3·10⁶, and the NIST-JANAF water-gas-shift equilibrium for reactors whose reverse rate comes from the equilibrium constant.

13 · Catalytic (LHHW / Hougen–Watson) rate laws

Rates of the form k(T)·[Π aorder − reverse]/(Σ Kt(T) Π ae)m, with a thermodynamically consistent driving force when the reverse rate comes from the equilibrium constant (the databank's or your own ln K correlation). References: the closed-form Langmuir–Hinshelwood plug-flow and stirred-tank solutions, and the published Xu & Froment (1989) steam-reforming model — three reversible reactions with negative hydrogen orders and a squared adsorption term — integrated independently with scipy, isothermal and adiabatic.

14 · Vapour association of carboxylic acids

With an activity-coefficient method, acids dimerise in the vapour (chemical theory: ideal gas of monomers, dimers and cross dimers). The measured vapour pressure and heat of vaporisation refer to this associated vapour, so the liquid enthalpy built from them is now consistent with the formation enthalpies — without association it is about 28 kJ/mol too high for acetic acid, which made liquid heats of reaction and adiabatic temperatures wrong. References: NIST liquid enthalpies of formation, the DIPPR vapour-pressure equation, and an independently written chemical-theory solution for vapour compressibilities.

15 · CO₂ absorption in aqueous MEA

The aqueous-MEA method solves the carbamate (2 MEA + CO₂ ⇌ MEAH⁺ + MEACOO⁻) and bicarbonate (MEA + CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ MEAH⁺ + HCO₃⁻) equilibria of the published Akula et al. model as implemented in the open-source IDAES process-modelling framework; CO₂ follows Henry's law on the free molecular CO₂ (N₂O analogy), water and MEA Raoult's law on the true species. Enthalpies come from the temperature dependence of the same fugacities, so the heat of absorption is consistent with the solubility. References: the IDAES property-package test values, an independent scipy solution of the published equations, and the IDAES heat of absorption.

Against measured vapour pressures

Total pressure over 30 wt % MEA (7.017 mol/kg water) measured by Arshad et al. (J. Chem. Eng. Data 59, 2014, 764; NIST ThermoML), against the engine's bubble pressure. At 120 °C the model is within 2 % up to a loading of 0.32 mol/mol and then over-predicts more and more (+19 % at 0.40, +37 % at 0.44); at 80 °C it is within 10 % to 0.44, and at 40 °C within 20 % at 0.5. Above about 0.55 it over-predicts the CO₂ pressure about twofold — a known limit of ideal-solution chemical-equilibrium models. In a regenerator this makes CO₂ look slightly easier to strip at the rich end, so reboiler duties come out somewhat low.

The pitzer.dat KHCO₃ parameters are fitted to about 3 mol/kg. In strong, highly converted solutions they make the model thermodynamically unstable (a spurious liquid–liquid split) close to where KHCO₃ would in fact crystallise; the engine maps that onset over 0–250 °C and, past 95 % of it, holds the properties at the boundary and extrapolates smoothly (the stream report flags such states). PHREEQC evaluates those states without a stability check, so they are listed separately and not graded — all are cold or 40 wt % solutions converted 60–90 % to bicarbonate, beyond normal hot-carbonate practice:

At high concentration the Pitzer water activity falls below the handbook's 20 °C vapour pressures (−8 % at 46 wt %) and the heat capacity of 40 wt % solution is 10 % low; between 20 and 30 wt % — the Benfield range — both agree within 1–4 %. The Pitzer parameters carry fitted temperature terms to about 90–100 °C and are extrapolated above that. Promoters (DEA, glycine, vanadium) change absorption rates, not the equilibrium, and are represented through tray efficiencies.

17 · Murphree tray efficiency

A tray with Murphree vapour efficiency E leaves its vapour at y = yin + E(K x − yin) instead of in equilibrium; the efficiency can be set for every tray or per component. Reference: the exact solution of the tray equations for a dilute absorber with a straight equilibrium line (numpy), which equals the Lewis–Kremser closed form. The regenerator case checks the condenser-temperature specification used for amine and carbonate strippers.

19 · Aqueous MDEA — Extended UNIQUAC

The Aqueous MDEA method is the Extended UNIQUAC electrolyte model (UNIQUAC + Debye–Hückel) with the parameter set of N. Sadegh's DTU PhD thesis (2013): true species H₂O, CO₂, MDEA, MDEAH⁺, H⁺, OH⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻; equilibrium constants from the fitted standard-state properties; CO₂ Henry constant of Rumpf & Maurer (1993). First check: the thesis printed the loading its model predicts at 110 kPa total pressure for 10–90 wt % MDEA at 40–80 °C; the engine solves the same condition (bubble pressure = 110 kPa) with the same parameters. The water vapour pressure comes from the databank rather than the model's own Cp integration, and the vapour is ideal rather than SRK, so agreement is to the printed two decimals, not to machine precision. Second check: an independent Python implementation of the model (scipy speciation) for the species distribution, and calorimetric heat of absorption.

The engine follows the thesis model's own deviation from these measurements point for point, as it should. The thesis explains the growth with temperature: the volume of CO₂ consumed in its cell shrinks as temperature rises, and at 80 °C a systematic error pulls all measured loadings down; below 70 wt % MDEA the model over-predicts solubility. The parameters were regressed to 1,597 literature points (pure MDEA, MDEA–water and CO₂–MDEA–water data) and represent the ternary data used within 16 % AARD; the stated validity range is 20–200 °C, CO₂ partial pressure up to 7,565 kPa, loading 0.0002–1.4 and 5–75 wt % MDEA. Piperazine-activated MDEA (aMDEA) is not part of this method yet — Neerup et al. (2025) give the MDEA–piperazine interaction parameters, but the piperazine species' standard-state data and UNIQUAC volume / area parameters they rest on are in Fosbøl et al. (2013), which is still to be added.

20 · Activated MDEA — piperazine added to the MDEA model

Piperazine (PZ) activates MDEA in most ammonia-plant CO₂ removal units. No complete, self-contained piperazine parameter set has been published for this model: the DTU group keeps its set in its consortium databank, and the University of Texas models depend on Aspen Plus databank values that are not printed. So the piperazine species were added here and fitted to measured data. Five species are added: PZ, PZH⁺, the carbamate PZCOO⁻, the protonated carbamate H⁺PZCOO⁻ and the dicarbamate PZ(COO)₂²⁻. The MDEA–CO₂–water part is the Sadegh (2013) set of section 19, unchanged.

  • PZ protonation: the constant comes from Gupta, da Silva & Svendsen (2022), whose correlation reproduces the measured pKa values plotted in their paper.
  • Interaction parameters: each piperazine species takes its UNIQUAC size, area and interaction parameters from the nearest Sadegh species: PZ and the zwitterion from MDEA, PZH⁺ from MDEAH⁺, the carbamate from HCO₃⁻ and the dicarbamate from CO₃²⁻.
  • Fitted values: five water interactions and the three carbamate reaction constants (each a value at 40 °C plus a reaction enthalpy) were regressed to the measured CO₂ pressures below, weighting the deviation in ln p(CO₂).
  • Held-out data: the 5 m MDEA / 5 m PZ data of Chen (2011) were kept out of the regression to test it.

Density of the loaded blends: piperazine and CO₂ apparent volumes were fitted to Frailie (2014, Table C-1). The largest deviation over its 31 points is 1.01 %. Limits of this extension:

  • Data range: the data reach 0.3 bar CO₂ below 100 °C and 0.45 mol/mol alkalinity, so the rich end of a high-pressure absorber is an extrapolation and the stream warnings say so. There, most of the CO₂ is held by MDEA, whose model is validated to 75 bar CO₂.
  • Speciation: the split of piperazine between its species is a by-product of fitting CO₂ pressures, not a measurement.
  • Heat of absorption: no calorimetric data were used. The heat implied by the temperature trend of the fitted CO₂ pressures sits within about 15 % of the trend in Xu's correlations at 80–120 °C. At 40 °C it deviates by up to about 30 %: higher at low loading, lower at high loading.

21 · Free water — water and steam on IAPWS-IF97 inside Peng–Robinson

With Peng–Robinson or SRK, the free-water option (on by default) refers the water in every liquid phase to IAPWS-IF97, and water vapour to IF97 at its partial pressure. Each case runs the engine's own heater, valve, pump or flash drum on pure water. Reference: IAPWS-95 (CoolProp 8.0.0); IF97 and IAPWS-95 agree to about 0.01 % here.

A plain cubic puts the latent heat of water about 2–5 % high below 100 bar and the fugacity of liquid water 10–15 % low near ambient (W7: too little water in the gas), and the error changes sign close to the critical point. Pure water alone saturates on a vapour-pressure correlation either way, and the pump uses the liquid density, so W6 is the same with and without free water. Mixtures are treated the same way: water in a liquid phase carries the IF97 correction in proportion to its mole fraction, and water vapour the IF97 residual at its partial pressure. Hydrocarbon liquids and dry gases are unchanged.

23 · Flash convergence near a critical point

2806 isothermal flashes of a natural-gas mixture (C1/C2/C3/nC5 = 80/10/6/4 mol %) over 200–260 K and 50–95 bar, which crosses its critical region. Successive substitution hands over to Newton–Raphson on ln K after 100 steps; every flash now reports whether it converged, and a unit with an unconverged flash says so in its results and on the status lamp.

24 · Energy-balance reconciliation

After every run the solver compares the enthalpy change from feeds to products with the sum of the unit duties and shaft work. A gap means two units evaluated the same stream on different enthalpy bases (a classic unit next to a property-method unit, or units with different property methods) or a recycle carried an error. It is flagged when it exceeds 0.1 % of the gross duty (at least 2 × 10⁻⁵ of the feed and product enthalpy flows, and 0.05 kW), and the warning names the units where the gap arises.

28 · Ammonia synthesis kinetics in fugacities

The kinetic plug-flow reactor takes rates in fugacities ai = yi φi P from the property method, and the Temkin–Pyzhev rate in the form of Dyson & Simon (1968): RNH₃ = η k [Ka² fN₂ (fH₂³/fNH₃²)α − (fNH₃²/fH₂³)1−α], k0 = 8.849·10¹⁴ kmol/(m³·h), E = 170.56 kJ/mol, α = 0.5, Ka of Gillespie & Beattie (1930). Reference: the same rate with thermo 0.6.1 PRMIX fugacity coefficients (engine constants and kij) integrated by scipy (Radau).

29 · Pipe segment

A pipe marched in segments with a P–H flash of the property method at each node: Darcy–Weisbach friction with the Churchill (1977) factor, elevation, acceleration and fittings, homogeneous two-phase flow, the API RP 14E erosional velocity and the Mach number of a gas. 30 · Urea synthesis method — Voskov et al. (2016)

The liquid is UNIQUAC over the true species NH₃, CO₂, H₂O, urea, ammonium carbamate and ammonium bicarbonate, with the carbamate and bicarbonate equilibria solved in every flash and urea formation solved by the urea reactor; parameters of Voskov, Pilaar & Rietveld (2016), the bicarbonate equilibrium constant refitted and no Poynting term in the chemical equilibria (the form that reproduces their tables); vapour Peng–Robinson with kij(NH₃–CO₂) = 0.10 fitted here. Reference: the paper's Table 8 (equilibrium conversion of the closed liquid) and Table 9 (its bubble pressure), every point.

Heats at 185 °C, 250 bar (all liquid): forming the liquid from NH₃, CO₂ and H₂O gases (N/C 3, H/C 0.5) -154.5 kJ per mol CO₂ — carbamate formation from the gases is about −117 to −159 kJ/mol, plus the solution of the excess ammonia; urea formation in the liquid 14.6 kJ per mol urea (the dehydration of carbamate to urea is endothermic, +15.5 kJ/mol in the literature). The urea HP synthesis example on the simulator page (adiabatic reactor at N/C 2.94, H/C 0.47) gives 56 % conversion at 185 °C and a stripping efficiency of 77 % with 0.83 t steam per t urea.

The worst bubble-pressure deviations are at N/C 2.5 and 200 °C, where the paper's own vapour model departs most from Peng–Robinson. Liquid density uses the model's partial molar volumes and liquid viscosity a log-mixing estimate — both indicative. Biuret and urea hydrolysis are not modelled.

31 · Machine performance curves and the multistage compressor

Pump and compressor curves (head, efficiency against flow at a rated speed) interpolated by monotone cubic Hermite; other speeds by the affinity laws Q ∝ N, H ∝ N². A pump's head sets the discharge pressure through ΔP = ρgH; a compressor's polytropic head sets the discharge pressure through the rigorous polytropic path of the property method, so Hp = ηpΔh. 34 · Solver transparency

Every run returns the history of each recycle loop — the largest relative change of the torn streams at every pass and how that pass was started — the final change of each torn stream, the design-spec Newton steps and the feedback-calculator passes; the simulator plots them in its Convergence tab. The recycle of vector MB-100 (mixer → shift reactor → cooler → flash → 50 / 50 splitter, tolerance 10⁻⁹) with each accelerator (S = direct substitution, W = Wegstein, B = Broyden):

Both accelerators land on the same recycle flow — the steady state does not depend on how it is reached. With a single torn stream, as here, Wegstein alone is as quick; Broyden's quasi-Newton update is meant for loops with several coupled torn streams, where Wegstein's one-variable-at-a-time steps ignore the coupling. The air rate reached is 45.1719 kg/h against 45.2024 kg/h frozen in the templates (vectors MB-276 to MB-279).

36 · Components from a structure, UNIFAC fill-in and transport properties

A component missing from the databank can be entered as a SMILES string. The structure is parsed (rings, aromaticity, charges, the five-valent nitro form normalised) and split into UNIFAC, Dortmund-UNIFAC and Joback groups by SMARTS matching with the priority algorithm of the open-source thermo library. Joback & Reid give Tb, Tc, Pc, Vc, ΔHf°, ΔGf° and the ideal-gas Cp; Lee–Kesler gives ω and the vapour pressure; the liquid density is Rackett through the Tyn–Calus volume at Tb. The few group assignments that differ from thermo over the large set are fused polycyclic hydrocarbons and quinodimethanes written in Kekulé form, where which rings count as aromatic is a convention. Group-contribution estimates are screening values: a large or strongly polar molecule can be off by more than the 90th percentile above, and Joback has no groups for some structures (formates, sulfones, furfural-type rings) — enter Tb, Tc and Pc for those. Estimated liquid viscosity is the weakest property; one measured value anchors it. Filled binary pairs are predictions, flagged in the run log and the property information; replace them with fitted data for design (vectors MB-291 to MB-305).

37 · Aqueous electrolytes and sour water

The aqueous-electrolyte method is the Pitzer (Harvie–Møller–Weare) model with the species, equilibrium constants, interaction parameters and mineral solubility products of the USGS PHREEQC pitzer.dat database for Na, K, Ca, Mg, Cl, S(VI), C(IV), H and O, unsymmetrical mixing (Eθ) for every pair of like-signed ions of different charge, and pH reported on the MacInnes scale. It is first checked against PHREEQC itself (20 solutions; 36 saturation indices) — the same data set, so this is a check of the implementation, not of the data:

Solids are not precipitated: a positive saturation index is reported and warned, and the solution stays supersaturated. pitzer.dat's CO₂(g) constant (Plummer & Busenberg 1982) is replaced by IAPWS G7-04 for CO₂ volatility — the two agree within 1 % below 50 °C and differ by 5–9 % at 100–150 °C. In the aqueous-electrolyte method only the CO₂ component can leave the liquid, so carbonate alkalinity that should decompose on boiling is entered as Na₂CO₃ or K₂CO₃ plus CO₂. The Laliberté heat-capacity, density and viscosity correlations are fitted to roughly 0–140 °C and are held at their range limits outside it. Sour-water results above 10 mol solute per kg water are extrapolated (vectors MB-306 to MB-326).

38 · Liquid enthalpy of the activity-coefficient methods

NRTL, UNIQUAC, Wilson, UNIFAC and the solvents of the electrolyte methods take their liquid enthalpy from liquid heat capacities: water on IAPWS-IF97, every other component with a liquid-Cp correlation anchored at its normal boiling point (saturated vapour on the package's vapour model minus ΔHvap) and carried by ∫Cp,L dT up to about 0.9 Tc. The older route, hig − ΔHvap(T), takes the liquid heat capacity from the slope of the ΔHvap correlation; it remains available (liquid_enthalpy: 'hvap', the default of DWSIM's activity methods). Most liquid-Cp correlations end near the normal boiling point and are extrapolated above it — at 0.8 Tc they are still within 2–9 % (acetone +9 %, ethanol +6 %); from 0.9 Tc the ΔHvap route takes over with its offset fading to zero at Tc. Components without a liquid-Cp correlation — mostly light gases and structure-only user components — stay on the ΔHvap route. The column-duty comparisons with DWSIM in section 22 are unchanged within their tolerance, because those columns run near the normal boiling points where both routes agree (vectors MB-327 to MB-332).

39 · Ternary maps, azeotrope search, multi-outlet separator and property-method options

Azeotropes. The azeotrope search scans every binary edge for sign changes of y − x, then solves ternary and quaternary azeotropes by Newton's method on y(x) − x = 0 from several starts; where an activity method predicts two liquids at the boiling point the bubble point is heterogeneous (liquid–liquid split, then the bubble condition of one liquid). “none” means the model does not form that azeotrope with its parameters. Water with benzene and cyclohexane uses the pairs fitted to IUPAC-NIST mutual solubilities in round 11 (section 40); before that ChemSep had none and the UNIFAC estimate failed for water–cyclohexane, so NRTL treated that pair as ideal. UNIQUAC's ChemSep pair for acetone–chloroform also puts a spurious tangent azeotrope 0.003 mol from pure acetone (56.14 °C) beside the real maximum-boiling one at 63.78 °C, and predicts ethanol–cyclohexane heterogeneous at its boiling point; both are properties of the parameter sets, reported as found.

Residue curve maps. Residue curves integrate dx/dξ = x − y (Heun's method, adaptive step). Pure components, azeotropes and the heterogeneous points are classified from the eigenvalues of d(x − y)/dx plus the transverse direction 1 − K∞ of the missing component; separatrices traced from the saddles are drawn as distillation boundaries. The component separator now takes up to eight outlets, each with its own temperature and pressure (or pressure and vapour fraction on the property method); its duty is the enthalpy of all outlets minus the feed, checked above against an independent heater and against the ideal-gas enthalpy change of the cooled outlet. The Poynting correction on the pure-liquid fugacity of the activity methods, exp[VL(P − Psat)/RT], was always applied and can now be switched off to match programs that omit it. Residue curve maps and the azeotrope search run within the 10-second limit of a single request for up to eight components; very large regions of liquid–liquid immiscibility take the longest (water–ethanol–benzene with NRTL about 0.1 s for the search, a few seconds for the full map) (vectors MB-333 to MB-351).

SRK binary parameters. SRK now has a kij table of its own (api/_lib/mb-bip-srk.js, built by scripts/build-srk-kij.py from ChemSep's DECHEMA SRK library; until this round SRK used the Peng–Robinson values). The library often lists several sets for one pair, some at cryogenic temperatures and a few far from the rest; the engine takes the median of the sets measured somewhere in 250–450 K, and the Peng–Robinson value where SRK has none in that range. DWSIM reads the same library but takes the first set listed and finds none for the pairs with N₂ or CO₂; given that set the engine reproduces DWSIM's SRK flash to 2×10⁻⁵ (case MB-389), so the two SRK equations are the same and only the kij differ.

DWSIM's rigorous distillation column could not be driven through the server (its stage connections are not set by the server's connect call); the engine column is checked against independent calculations in sections 22 and 27.

Water–hydrocarbon pairs. ChemSep has no NRTL or UNIQUAC parameters for water with hydrocarbons. Until this round the engine estimated them from UNIFAC — water in benzene came out more than twice the data, and water–toluene and water–alkane pairs failed the estimate's fit test and were treated as ideal, so those mixtures formed a single liquid. The pairs for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, the xylenes, cyclohexane, methylcyclohexane, C5–C8 n-alkanes and isooctane are now fitted (scripts/fit-water-hydrocarbon.py, Aspen form τ = a + b/T + e ln T, NRTL α = 0.2) to both liquid phases of the IUPAC-NIST reference mutual solubilities from 0 °C to 120–200 °C: the SDS-81 smoothing equations for the hydrocarbon in water, and for water in the hydrocarbon the SDS-81 reference equations (toluene and ethylbenzene from the IUPAC Technical Report of Bazyleva & Acree, 2021; alkanes from Mączyński et al., J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 33, 2004), the xylenes anchored at the recommended 25 °C value and benzene fitted to the IUPAC recommended values 25–70 °C. Mole fractions; worst deviation from the reference 4.5 % (NRTL) and 7.4 % (UNIQUAC). With these pairs the water–ethanol–benzene layers at the ternary heteroazeotrope fall on the tabulated ones (upper 0.8 / 12.5 / 86.7 against 1.3 / 12.7 / 86.0 wt % water / ethanol / benzene, lower 43.4 / 50.9 / 5.8 against 43.1 / 52.1 / 4.8), and the heteroazeotropes of water with benzene, toluene and cyclohexane come within 0.5 K and 0.2 wt % of the CRC values (69.3, 84.1 and 69.8 °C). The vapour of the ternary heteroazeotrope carries 22 wt % ethanol against 18.5 tabulated (64.3 °C against 64.9 °C) — that part is set by the ChemSep ethanol pairs.

Volume translation. Peng–Robinson puts the molar volume of H₂, He, N₂, O₂, Ar, CH₄ and CO 3–7 cm³/mol low. The engine now shifts it by constants fitted to the reference equations of state in CoolProp (Péneloux et al. 1982; volume_translation: false turns it off). The shift is consistent: enthalpy moves by −P Σxici and fugacity coefficients by −ciP/RT, so phase equilibria are unchanged and reaction equilibria move as the real-gas non-ideality requires. Compressed liquids. Liquid densities from the density correlations, Rackett and COSTALD now carry the Thomson–Brobst–Hankinson (Tait) pressure correction, and a light gas dissolved below 10 mol % in a liquid takes a partial molar volume (about half its critical volume) instead of switching the whole liquid to COSTALD. An ammonia-loop separator liquid (2 mol % dissolved H₂, N₂, CH₄, Ar at 0 °C, 140 bar) now comes out at 638 kg/m³ against 622 before; pure ammonia at those conditions is 647.7 (DWSIM's default, which mixes mass densities with mole fractions, gives 658). The Tait correction over-predicts the pressure effect of the n-alkanes by about a fifth at 500 bar (1.3 % on density) and under-predicts that of methanol (1.8 % at 300 bar). Ammonia liquid thermal conductivity now follows the reference correlation (the generic correlation was 15 % low).

Heterogeneous bubble points with an equation of state. Nitrogen with ethane, propane or CO₂ near the critical pressure of nitrogen is two liquids below its bubble point — a nitrogen-rich and a heavy one — and the first vapour forms when the nitrogen-rich liquid boils. The bubble-point solver now checks whether the feed, taken as one liquid, would split; if it does, the bubble point is found as the temperature at which the lighter liquid of the split is at its own bubble point, so that three phases coexist (cases MB-392 to MB-395). Before, these cases either failed or returned the bubble point of the unstable single liquid, as DWSIM does — for nitrogen–ethane at 30 bar with DWSIM's SRK parameters 124.86 K against 124.87 K with the split, but at 10 bar with Peng–Robinson 101.0 K against 104.3 K, where the split is wide. Solids are not modelled.

41 · Extended component databank

The property methods draw on 1,549 pure components: the 431 of the ChemSep databank and 1,118 added in round 12 (388 oxygenate, 294 halogenated, 222 hydrocarbon, 138 nitrogen, 48 sulfur, 28 inorganic). Every added compound has tabulated critical constants (IUPAC critical-property series, Matthews, CRC Handbook, DIPPR 801 as published by Pina-Martinez et al. 2019, PSRK tables) and a tabulated normal boiling point; 57 fluids with a reference equation of state (refrigerants, siloxanes, others) take their constants and curves from it. The data were compiled from the published sources in the open-source chemicals, CoolProp and thermo libraries (MIT licence) by scripts/gather-compdb-ext.py; scripts/build-compdb-ext.mjs checks them and writes api/_lib/mb-compdb-ext.js. “Anchored”: Rackett density through the CRC Handbook density at 20 °C. Vapour pressures counted as measured include 656 Antoine equations (Landolt–Börnstein, NIST WebBook, Poling et al.) that cover only part of the curve and were refitted as DIPPR eq. 101 through their own points, the boiling point and the critical point. 8 compounds have no measured or estimable ΔHf and are flagged “no ΔHf” in the program (fine in heat and material balances, not in reactions). Estimated values use the same methods as a component given by its structure (Joback, Lee–Kesler through the measured Tb, Tc, Pc, Riedel–Watson, Rackett through the Tyn–Calus volume). UNIFAC and Dortmund groups are the DDBST assignments where they exist; the engine’s own fragmentation of the structure agrees with them for 889 of 892 compounds (UNIFAC) and 874 of 895 (Dortmund).

Checks before a compound goes in. The structure must give the formula the data are filed under; tabulated boiling points that disagree (they do by several kelvin now and then) are decided by a vapour-pressure equation covering the boiling point, which must reach 1 atm within 3 K of one of them, or else by agreement of two sources within 1.5 K; conflicting critical constants are decided by agreement with the Joback estimate, and a lone value far from it is not used; every correlation must stay inside physical limits at a temperature in its range (heat capacity rising with T and within 25 % of Joback, Trouton ratio 20–160 J/(mol K), density 300–3500 kg/m³ and falling with T, and so on). 192 compounds were left out:

  • 59 — no ideal-gas heat capacity (none measured and no group-contribution estimate)
  • 51 — critical constants from DIPPR only and no vapour-pressure equation that passes the checks
  • 49 — no tabulated normal boiling point
  • 19 — critical constant far from the group-contribution estimate and not confirmed by a second source
  • 13 — duplicate (stereo-isomer, or second CAS number of a ChemSep component)
  • 1 — acentric factor outside −0.4 to 1.6 (inconsistent constants)

126 correlations failed their check and were replaced by the next source or the estimate (116 vapour pressure, 9 ideal-gas heat capacity, 1 liquid density). Before the databank was assembled this way, 434 compounds with DIPPR critical constants but no measured boiling point and vapour pressure were already excluded, as were compounds with metals or other elements outside C, H, O, N, S, the halogens, P, Si, B and the noble gases, salts, and molecules above 500 g/mol.

How good the estimates are. Where a compound has a measured value, the estimate it would otherwise get was compared with it: vapour pressure by Lee–Kesler through Tb, Tc, Pc — median 2.7 %, one point in ten off by more than 15.5 % (4371 points, 0.55–0.95 Tc); Joback ideal-gas heat capacity — median 0.5 %, 90th percentile 4.6 %; Rackett density through the Tyn–Calus volume — median 2.0 %, 90th percentile 7.3 %; Riedel–Watson heat of vaporisation at Tb — median 2.0 %, 90th percentile 9.2 %. Two independent measured vapour-pressure equations for the same compound (139 compounds, above 1 kPa) differ by a median 0.6 % at their worst point — the spread of the data themselves.

42 · GERG-2008 and the reference equations of state

GERG-2008 (Kunz & Wagner, J. Chem. Eng. Data 57 (2012) 3032; ISO 20765-2) is the reference equation for natural gas and its 21 components — methane to n-decane, N₂, CO₂, H₂, O₂, CO, H₂O, H₂S, He and Ar. The engine's version (api/_lib/mb-gerg.js) is generated by scripts/gen-gerg2008.py from NIST's public-domain AGA 8 code; fugacity coefficients for phase equilibrium come from the analytic composition derivative of the Helmholtz energy (checked against central differences to 1e-8, and Σ xi ln φi equals the residual Gibbs energy to 1e-15). GERG-2008 and the reference equations take their ideal-gas heat capacities from the equations themselves, placed on the same enthalpy and entropy basis as the other methods at 25 °C, so a stream keeps its enthalpy when it passes between units on different methods. Viscosity and thermal conductivity still come from the databank correlations. A GERG-2008 phase envelope takes a few seconds (the Helmholtz equation is far more expensive than a cubic).

43 · Refinery methods: Peng–Robinson 1978, PRSV2, Lee–Kesler–Plöcker, Chao–Seader and Grayson–Streed

Peng–Robinson 1978 differs from Peng–Robinson only in α(ω) for components with ω above 0.491 (heavy hydrocarbons and petroleum fractions). PRSV2 (Stryjek & Vera 1986) gives each component α = [1 + κ(1 − √Tr)]² with κ = κ0(ω) + [κ1 + κ2(κ3 − Tr)(1 − √Tr)](1 + √Tr)(0.7 − Tr) below Tr = 0.7. The engine's κ1–κ3 are not the published table: scripts/build-prsv2.mjs fits them to the databank vapour pressure of every component that has one (1241 of them) — the α that makes Peng–Robinson reproduce the vapour pressure exactly, at 40 temperatures from the triple point (or 0.35 Tc) to 0.7 Tc, by linear least squares. Vapour pressures from the equation itself (equal fugacities) against the databank correlation:

TrComponentsPRSV2 medianPRSV2 90th pct.Peng–Robinson medianPeng–Robinson 90th pct.
0.512010.046 %0.52 %12.65 %44.3 %
0.612410.022 %0.57 %4.06 %17.8 %
0.712410.022 %2.40 %0.41 %5.8 %
0.812411.865 %11.09 %2.00 %11.8 %
0.912392.340 %15.18 %2.45 %16.0 %

Above Tr = 0.7 the κ1–κ3 term is zero, as Stryjek and Vera prescribe, so PRSV2 is only as good as the acentric factor there — the same as Peng–Robinson. Where the databank vapour-pressure curve and the critical constants disagree, both show it at high Tr.

Lee–Kesler–Plöcker (Lee & Kesler 1975; Plöcker, Knapp & Prausnitz 1978): the simple-fluid and n-octane reference BWR equations in reduced variables, Plöcker's pseudo-critical mixing rules with η = 0.25, hydrogen with the Gunn–Chueh–Prausnitz quantum-corrected constants. Fugacity coefficients come from the analytic composition derivative through Tr, Pr and ω (checked against central differences of n·GR/RT to 5e-9). Plöcker's own kij table is not freely available, so scripts/fit-lkp-kij.mjs fits kij (the multiplier on Tc,ij) for each pair of the GERG-2008 components that has fitted GERG-2008 mixture parameters — water and helium left out — to GERG-2008 bubble pressures at three temperatures and three compositions below 100 bar: 130 pairs, median mean absolute deviation in bubble pressure 1.5 % (one pair in ten above 9 %), against 28 % with kij = 1. Other pairs take correlations fitted to that table: hydrocarbon pairs k = 1 + a lnτ lnν + b lnτ + c (lnτ)² (τ, ν the Tc and Vc ratios; 49 pairs, rms 0.016), and a line in ln(Tc,HC/Tc,gas) for each of N₂, CO₂, CO, H₂, methane, ethane and propane with heavier hydrocarbons. C2H6 – n-nonane and n-nonane – n-pentane lay far off the homologous trend (GERG-2008 rests on sparse data there) and take the correlation instead. Examples:

Methane, nitrogen and CO₂ with the heavier alkanes and hydrogen with any hydrocarbon keep deviations of 5–18 %: a single kij cannot follow GERG-2008's temperature dependence there. For hydrogen with hydrocarbons, Chao–Seader or Grayson–Streed is the better choice.

Chao–Seader and Grayson–Streed (Chao & Seader 1961; Grayson & Streed 1963): K = ν γ / φV with the corresponding-states liquid fugacity coefficient ν (simple fluid plus ω term, hydrogen and methane with constants of their own), the Scatchard–Hildebrand regular solution with the solubility parameters and 25 °C liquid volumes (31 and 52 cm³/mol for hydrogen and methane), and a Redlich–Kwong vapour. Liquid enthalpy and entropy come from Lee–Kesler with Plöcker mixing, as commercial simulators do — the temperature derivative of ν gives heat capacities 10–20 % low.

Bubble and dew pressures of equation-of-state mixtures now fall back on a scan of PT flashes in pressure when the Newton solution fails or lands on the trivial one, as bubble and dew temperatures already did — a light gas dissolved in a heavy liquid above its critical temperature (methane in n-hexane at 355 K) had no bubble pressure before. 44 · UNIFAC-LL, NIST-modified UNIFAC and the viscosity of aqueous MDEA

UNIFAC-LL (Magnussen, Rasmussen & Fredenslund, Ind. Eng. Chem. Process Des. Dev. 20 (1981) 331) is original UNIFAC with interaction parameters fitted to liquid–liquid equilibria — 57 subgroups in 32 main groups, temperature-independent amn, propanols as groups of their own. NIST-modified UNIFAC (Kang, Diky & Frenkel, Fluid Phase Equilib. 388 (2015) 128) is the Dortmund form with groups and parameters refitted to critically evaluated data — 201 subgroups, including branched ketones, ring ethers and amines, aromatic acids and esters. Both tables come from the thermo library (MIT licence; scripts/gen-unifac2.py, one typo in its UNIFAC-LL table corrected: R of the ring CH₂O group is 0.9183). The engine's activity coefficients equal thermo's with the same groups to 1.2e-15 (9 mixtures). Groups come from each component's structure with the SMARTS of each table: 965 of the 1549 databank components get UNIFAC-LL groups (948 from the structure, 17 mapped from their UNIFAC groups; the rest contain groups UNIFAC-LL does not have — amines, sulfur, fluorine — and are treated with the combinatorial term only, as the run log says), 1400 get NIST groups; for 167 of them the NIST assignment differs from the Dortmund one because NIST has the finer group. Components added by structure take the groups mapped from their UNIFAC and Dortmund assignments.

No version is best everywhere. UNIFAC-LL puts the 1-butanol–water layers within a few per cent of the measurements and benzene, toluene and ethylbenzene within about 25 % both ways, where Dortmund and NIST UNIFAC put 2–3 times too much water into the aromatics; but UNIFAC-LL makes ethyl acetate and methyl ethyl ketone 2–3 times too insoluble in water, and every version over-predicts alkanes in water by an order of magnitude or more. UNIFAC-LL is also the poorest of the four for vapour–liquid equilibrium (ethanol–water bubbles about 2 K high), so it is meant for extraction and decanters, not distillation. None of them replaces NRTL fitted to solubility data for a decanter design.

Viscosity of aqueous MDEA and activated MDEA. The Aqueous MDEA method had no liquid viscosity until now (reported as unavailable). It now uses the form of Weiland et al. (J. Chem. Eng. Data 43 (1998) 378), ln(μ/μw) = W[(aW + b)T + (cW + d)][1 + α(fT + g)]/T² (W mass % amine on a CO₂-free basis, α mol CO₂ per mol amine), with a–d fitted here to Arachchige, Aryal, Eimer & Melaaen, Annual Transactions of the Nordic Rheology Society 21 (2013): aqueous MDEA 10–60 mass %, 293–353 K (48 points, mean deviation 1.4 %, largest 5.3 %) and f, g to Fluid Phase Equilib. (2015), DOI 10.1016/j.fluid.2015.06.034 (NIST ThermoML archive): 45 mass % MDEA with CO2, 303–363 K, loadings from the solubility data of the same paper (23 points up to α = 0.85, mean deviation 3.9 % on μ(α)/μ(0)). Piperazine is counted as MDEA by mass — an estimate. The liquid now also reports a pH from the H⁺ molality of the speciation (activity coefficient taken as 1). 45 · Stream properties: Cv, Cp/Cv, speed of sound and the Joule–Thomson coefficient

The stream-properties view reports, for each phase, the derived properties of the equation of state alongside density, enthalpy, entropy and Cp. They come from the phase volume V(T, P, x) by central differences: Cv = Cp − T(∂V/∂T)P2 / [−(∂V/∂P)T]; the speed of sound w = √[(Cp/Cv) / (ρ κT)] with κT = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T; and μJT = [T(∂V/∂T)P − V] / Cp. A vapour gets all four from any method. A liquid gets μJT from any method, but Cv, Cp/Cv and w only from Steam / water, the reference equations and GERG-2008: liquid-density correlations (Rackett, COSTALD) fix the density well but not its pressure derivative, and give liquid compressibilities several times too large. The Steam / water method takes w directly from IAPWS-IF97. The mixture Cp of a two-phase stream is the slope of the flash enthalpy and includes the latent heat. The bubble and dew points shown with the stream are the same bubble- and dew-point flashes as the phase envelopes of section 10.

46 · Energy streams

An energy stream carries heat or shaft work from one unit to another, as in other sequential-modular simulators: the unit at the arrow head takes the energy the unit at the tail gives up as its own specification — its duty (heater, mixer, flash drum, three-phase separator) or its shaft power (compressor). The solver treats each link as a calculator: receiving duty = −(source duty or work) × fraction delivered, run after the source and before the receiver, or, when the receiver lies upstream of the source in the same process, converged by repeated passes around the flowsheet. An arrow with no source gives a duty you type in; an arrow with no receiver only reports the source’s duty. Heat goes to heat and work to work; turbines, pumps and exchangers cannot receive energy streams, and both refusals are tested.

47 · Free water beside a liquid hydrocarbon

With Peng–Robinson or SRK, free water puts liquid water on IAPWS-IF97 (section 21) and moves the infinite-dilution fugacity of each dissolved gas onto its Henry constant (section 22). The Henry term was written as an excess Gibbs energy G/RT = xw·Σ xgΔg, exact in water but symmetric: it also gave water dissolved in a hydrocarbon-rich liquid ln γ = Σ xgΔg, about −6 for propane, so water became hundreds of times too soluble in liquid propane and in the condensate of a wet gas. The term is now G/RT = Σ xgΔg·xwσ(xw), with σ a smooth step from 0 at xw = 0.5 to 1 in pure water: unchanged at infinite dilution and to first order in the gas concentration (sections 21, 22 and 40 are unchanged to the printed digits; two sour-water deviations of section 37, which use the Peng–Robinson vapour, move by one percentage point), and zero in a water-poor liquid, which keeps the cubic’s own water solubility. A phase with a single real root of the equation of state is labelled by what it is — gas above its pseudo-critical temperature (Li’s rule), liquid below it when dense — instead of by which of two tied candidates the three-phase flash kept.

Structural checks: liquid propane at 69.5 bar is far above its vapour pressure, so propane + water has no vapour; a gas of C₁–C₄ alone is single-phase at 15 °C and 69.5 bar, so the only liquid it can drop is water. The water left in the propane liquid, about 1 mol %, is the constant-kij cubic’s value and is higher than measured (see Scope). Flowsheets with wet gas and a condensing hydrocarbon (C₃+ liquids, condensate, LPG) solved before this fix overstated the condensate and the cooler duties that come with it; run them again.

Scope

These checks verify the implementation against independent references. Agreement with another simulator shows the equations are solved correctly for the given parameters; it does not make a property method suitable for every system — Peng–Robinson without fitted kij over-predicts the solubility of water in hydrocarbon liquids, ChemSep NRTL / UNIQUAC parameters are fitted to vapour–liquid data, and the classic urea units remain empirical correlations (the urea synthesis method of section 30 is the rigorous alternative). Use the results for preliminary engineering and confirm them against plant data before design use. Kinetic reactors are only as good as the rate expressions entered, and the acid association model covers dimerisation only (no acid–water cross association; binary parameters fitted without association may need refitting). The CO₂ packages cover CO₂ only (H₂S and NH₃ chemistry is the sour-water method of section 37), the piperazine part of activated MDEA is a fit to measured CO₂ pressures (section 20), and tray efficiencies stand in for rate-based mass transfer. The Steam / water method takes pure water only. Sections 21–47 are generated by this page's build script from the references in tests/validation-references.json. Peng–Robinson has no built-in kij for H₂–NH₃ or CH₄–NH₃; calibrate them against plant separator data for ammonia-loop work. The inputs for every other case above are in the engine test set, cases MB-089 to MB-449.
